claims.text: The initial alloy is equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The initial alloy is single-phase and has a uniform microstructure without significant solute clustering or intermetallic phases.
Isothermal aging at 600–800 °C can be tuned to induce nanoscale solute clustering without causing conventional intermetallic precipitation.
An argon atmosphere prevents oxidation during aging.
Thermally activated solute diffusion produces nanoscale clusters in aged CoCrFeMnNi.
The nanoscale solute clusters form both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Nanoscale solute clusters locally reduce bonding or cohesive strength.
Nanoscale solute clusters act as local stress concentrators under mechanical loading.
Cluster-associated stress concentration promotes premature crack nucleation.
Cluster-associated crack nucleation causes a transition toward brittle failure even while the bulk microstructure remains single-phase.
The as-cast, unaged alloy has a uniform microstructure and high toughness.
Controlled aging will reduce strain-to-failure relative to the as-cast baseline.
Controlled aging will reduce toughness relative to the as-cast baseline.
The observed nanoscale clusters will correlate spatially with localized embrittlement and early crack initiation.
High-resolution TEM and EBSD mapping will reveal the nanoscale clustering associated with embrittlement.
Aging beyond the tuned conditions may produce conventional intermetallic precipitation or other degradation phenomena.
The proposed embrittlement mechanism is limited to aging conditions that create clustering without intermetallic precipitation.
The clustering hypothesis would be falsified if detectable clusters form without a significant loss of toughness or change in fracture mode.
